column1: # Written by Claude (origin "claude"). One line per entry:  entry id|typical learner mistake|usage note
# Notes are in English. Either text column may be empty.
en:do:verb|"Do" is for tasks and activities, "make" for producing something: "do your homework", "do the dishes", but "make a cake", "make a mistake", "make a decision".|
en:make:verb|"Make a mistake", "make a decision", "make a cake", but "do homework", "do the dishes", "do sport".|
en:say:verb|"Say" takes the words, "tell" takes the person: "She said hello", "She told me the news". Not "she said me".|
en:tell:verb|"Tell" needs the person: "tell me", "tell him the truth". Fixed exceptions: "tell a story", "tell the truth", "tell a lie".|
en:actually:adverb|"Actually" means "in fact", not "at the moment". For that use "currently" or "now" (German aktuell, French actuellement, Portuguese atualmente).|
en:eventually:adverb|"Eventually" means "in the end, after a long time", not "possibly". For "possibly" use "perhaps" (German eventuell, French éventuellement, Portuguese eventualmente).|
en:sensible:adjective|"Sensible" means reasonable (German vernünftig). Someone who is easily hurt is "sensitive" (German sensibel, French sensible).|
en:become:verb|"Become" means German "werden", not "bekommen". "To get" or "to receive" is bekommen.|
en:information:noun|Uncountable: "some information", "a piece of information", not "an information" or "informations".|
en:advice:noun|Uncountable: "some advice", "a piece of advice", not "an advice". The verb is spelled with s: "to advise".|
en:since:preposition|"Since" + a starting point (since 2020, since Monday); "for" + a length of time (for two years). Both with the present perfect: "I have lived here for two years".|
en:borrow:verb|"Borrow" is to take for a while, "lend" is to give for a while: "Can I borrow your pen?" / "Can you lend me your pen?"|
en:lend:verb|"Lend" is to give for a while, "borrow" is to take: "Can you lend me ten francs?"|
en:fun:noun|"Fun" means enjoyable, "funny" means it makes you laugh: "The party was fun", "the joke was funny".|
en:funny:adjective|"Funny" makes you laugh or is strange; something you enjoy is "fun": "We had fun".|
en:remember:verb|"Remember" is to keep in mind; "remind" is to make someone remember: "Remind me to call her".|
en:remind:verb|"Remind someone to do something" or "remind someone of something": "You remind me of my brother".|
en:control:verb|"Control" means to steer or have power over. To look whether something is right is "check": "check the tickets" (German kontrollieren, French contrôler).|
en:gift:noun|In English a gift is a present. Careful: German "Gift" means poison.|
en:chef:noun|A chef is a professional cook, not a boss (German Chef, French chef = boss).|
en:handy:adjective|"Handy" means useful or practical. A mobile phone is a "mobile phone" or "cell phone" (German Handy).|
en:pretend:verb|"Pretend" means to act as if something were true, not "to intend" (French prétendre = to claim, Spanish and Portuguese pretender = to intend).|
en:assist:verb|"Assist" means to help. To be present at an event is "attend" (French assister à, Spanish asistir a).|
en:attend:verb|"Attend" means to be present at (a meeting, a school), not "to wait" (French attendre) or "to serve" (Spanish atender).|
en:library:noun|A library lends books; a shop that sells them is a bookshop or bookstore (French librairie, Spanish librería, Portuguese livraria).|
en:actual:adjective|"Actual" means real, not current: "the actual price" is the real price. Current = "current".|
en:will:verb|"Will" makes the future: "I will go". To want is "want" (German "ich will" = I want).|
en:their:determiner|"Their" (possessive), "there" (place) and "they're" (they are) sound the same.|
en:than:conjunction|"Than" compares (taller than me); "then" is about time (first ..., then ...).|
en:much:determiner|"Much" goes with uncountable nouns (much water, much time), "many" with plurals (many books).|
en:many:determiner|"Many" goes with plurals (many people), "much" with uncountable nouns (much money).|
en:get:verb||"Get" has many uses: receive (get a letter), become (get tired), arrive (get home), understand (I get it).
en:a:article|"A" before a consonant sound, "an" before a vowel sound: a university, a one-way street, an hour, an umbrella.|
en:wish:verb|"I wish" + past is for things that are not true now: "I wish I had more time". For the future use "hope": "I hope you win".|
en:listen:verb|"Listen to" someone or something; "hear" is what reaches your ears without trying: "I heard a noise, so I listened".|
en:watch:verb|"Watch" is for things that move or change (TV, a match); "look at" for still things (a picture); "see" is just perceiving.|
en:lose:verb|"Lose" has one o (I lost my keys). "Loose", with two, means not tight.|
en:bring:verb|"Bring" is toward the speaker, "take" is away: "Bring me a coffee", "Take this to your mother".|
en:learn:verb|"Learn" is what the student does, "teach" what the teacher does: "She teaches me German", not "she learns me".|
en:already:adverb|"Already" in questions shows surprise: "Are you done already?" "Yet" is for negatives and neutral questions: "Not yet", "Are you done yet?"|
en:during:preposition|"During" + a noun (during the film), "while" + a clause (while I was watching), "for" + a length of time (for two hours).|
en:people:noun|"People" is plural: "people are", not "people is". One person, two people. "A people" (singular) means a nation.|
en:news:noun|Singular despite the -s: "The news is good", not "the news are".|
en:boring:adjective|"Boring" describes the thing, "bored" describes how you feel: "The film was boring, so I was bored". "I am boring" means others find you dull.|
en:its:determiner|"Its" is possessive (the dog wagged its tail); "it's" is short for "it is" or "it has".|
en:interesting:adjective|"Interesting" describes the thing, "interested" the person: "The book is interesting", "I am interested in history".|
en:thanks:interjection||"Thanks" is a little more casual than "thank you". Answer with "You're welcome" or "No problem".
